entries.name: Ontario Autism Program (OAP)
entries.description: The Ontario Autism Program offers support to families of children and youth on the autism spectrum, until age 18. A child must be under 18, live in Ontario and have a written diagnosis of autism from a qualified professional, and families register through AccessOAP and provide the supporting documents it asks for.
entries.cost_note: The page does not mention fees for registering or for services.
entries.evidence: Register for the Ontario Autism Program through AccessOAP and provide all supporting documentation that they ask for.
entries.notes: Phone and email are AccessOAP's, as printed on this page. The page also lists the ministry's Central Resource Team (oap@ontario.ca, 1-888-444-4530) and Autism Ontario (1-800-472-7789). Page updated April 16, 2026.

entries.name: AccessOAP
entries.description: AccessOAP is the independent intake organization funded by the Government of Ontario to help families register for and access the supports and services of the Ontario Autism Program. Families can apply online, by mail or by phone, and care coordinators help them choose services and guide them through the determination of needs process for core clinical services.
entries.cost_note: No registration fee is mentioned; the OAP Services page says registered families can access Foundational Family Services at no cost.
entries.evidence: Families have access to care coordinators who can help them navigate the system
entries.notes: accessoap.ca failed WebFetch's certificate check, so its pages were fetched with curl (HTTP 200) on 2026-10-17. Phone hours: Monday to Friday, 8:30am to 5pm Eastern Time. Email is from the Contact Us page (accessoap.ca/contact-us/), which also lists TTY 1.800.855.1155. Operated by Accerta Services Inc. The diagnosis letter must include the child's full name and date of birth, the assessment date, a statement that the child meets the criteria for autism spectrum disorder, and the professional's name and credentials.

entries.name: Assistance for Children with Severe Disabilities (ACSD)
entries.description: Ontario financial support to help parents and guardians with the costs of caring for a child under 18 with a severe disability, paying between $25 and $678 a month. Families with a total household income of $77,640 or less may be eligible, and can apply online (with 90 days to finish) or send a paper form to a local ministry regional office.
entries.cost_note: Benefit paid to families; the page does not mention any fee to apply.
entries.evidence: Eligible parents and guardians can receive between $25 and $678 a month to help with disability-related costs.
entries.notes: Family size, the severity of the disability and extraordinary disability-related costs are also considered. No phone or email on the page; it links to a Contact us page and local ministry regional offices. Page updated June 30, 2026.

entries.name: Special Services at Home (SSAH)
entries.description: Ontario funding that helps families caring for a child under 18 with a developmental and/or physical disability pay for respite, support for daily activities, and activities of growth and development. A regulated health professional must document the child's functional limitations, and families apply online (with 90 days to finish) or mail a paper application to their local ministry regional office.
entries.cost_note: Funding program; the page does not mention any fee. It says SSAH is discretionary and funding is provided according to available resources.
entries.evidence: helps families taking care of a child with a developmental and/or physical disability
entries.notes: Basic living expenses such as food, housing and private school tuition are not covered. For infants and young children without a definitive diagnosis, a health professional's written statement about a likely delay can be used, with eligibility reviewed at about age 6. The page lists MyDirectPlan support (1-844-637-6371, support@MyDirectPlan.com) for submitting expenses online; SSAH questions go to the local ministry regional office.

entries.name: Passport Program
entries.description: Ontario funding that helps adults 18 or older with a developmental disability take part in their communities, and helps their caregivers take a break. Eligible people get base funding of $5,665 a year (up to $45,604), apply through Developmental Services Ontario, and are reimbursed for admissible expenses from the invoices and receipts they submit.
entries.cost_note: Funding program; the page does not mention any fee.
entries.evidence: Passport is a reimbursement program where people and families submit invoices and receipts for admissible expenses.
entries.notes: The page says a developmental disability should be determined by a psychologist or psychological associate. Applicants must live in Ontario and either still be in school and need help joining their community, or have left school and live with family or in supported independent living. Funding can also be received directly or as supports from an agency. The page lists phone numbers for each region's Passport agency. Page updated September 10, 2026.

entries.name: Developmental Services Ontario (DSO)
entries.description: DSO is the access point for adult developmental services and supports funded by the Ministry of Children, Community and Social Services, including Passport funding; it does not deliver services itself. Applicants gather proof of a developmental disability (a written psychological assessment), Ontario residency and age, apply online or by phone, and then meet an assessor twice to complete the application package.
entries.cost_note: The pages do not mention a fee to apply; the FAQ notes that people without a psychological assessment can pay a psychologist or psychological associate for one.
entries.evidence: The assessor will set up two meetings with you to help you complete an application package
entries.notes: People can be confirmed eligible at age 16, although services do not start until after age 18. Each assessor meeting is about three hours, with at least two people who know the applicant well. The first phone call takes up to 30 minutes. No phone or email on the page; contact the area DSO through the site. The Passport Program page says to contact DSO to apply for Passport funding.

entries.name: Ontario Disability Support Program (ODSP)
entries.description: ODSP provides income support, benefits for health costs and other disability supports for people in Ontario who have a disability and are in financial need. Apply online (about 20 to 30 minutes), by phone through the Social Assistance Support Line, or in person by booking an appointment at a local ODSP office.
entries.cost_note: Income support program; the page does not mention any fee to apply.
entries.evidence: The application takes 20 to 30 minutes.
entries.notes: Phone is the Social Assistance Support Line; TTY 1-800-387-5559. Eligibility looks at household income, assets and living costs, and whether the person meets the legislative definition of a person with a disability. The page says the Canada Disability Benefit will not affect ODSP eligibility or payment amount. Employment supports have a separate application. Page updated September 23, 2026.

entries.name: Assistive Devices Program (ADP)
entries.description: The Assistive Devices Program helps Ontario residents with long-term physical disabilities pay for customized equipment and specialized supplies, in categories such as mobility aids, communication aids, hearing devices and visual aids. Applicants need a valid Ontario health card and a physical disability that needs the equipment for 6 months or longer; income is not considered, and each category's page explains how to qualify, apply and find a vendor.
entries.cost_note: For fixed-price equipment ADP pays 75% of the approved price and you pay the remaining 25%; for people on Ontario Works or ODSP, ADP can pay up to 100%, depending on the funding model.
entries.evidence: ADP will pay 75% of the approved price
entries.notes: Also 416-327-8804; TTY 1-800-387-5559. Mailing address printed on the page: 5700 Yonge Street, 7th Floor, Toronto, Ontario, M2M 4K5. Not available if WSIB or Veterans Affairs Canada already covers the same equipment. Page updated March 26, 2026.

entries.name: Canada Disability Benefit
entries.description: A federal benefit that provides direct financial support to people with disabilities aged 18 to 64. Applicants must be approved for the Disability Tax Credit and have filed their taxes (with their spouse or partner, if any), and can apply online, by phone, in person at a Service Canada office or with a printed form, with help from someone they trust.
entries.cost_note: Federal benefit; the pages do not mention any fee to apply.
entries.evidence: provides direct financial support to people with disabilities who are between 18 and 64 years old
entries.notes: Also checked the Do you qualify and How to apply pages (…/canada-disability-benefit/eligibility.html and …/apply.html). You can apply up to 6 months before your 18th birthday; you and any spouse or partner must have filed your 2025 federal income tax return; Canadian citizens, permanent residents, people registered or entitled to be registered under the Indian Act, protected persons, and temporary residents who have lived in Canada for the previous 18 months can qualify. A legal representative can apply for someone else. No phone number is printed on these pages. Page dated 2026-09-10.

entries.name: Disability Tax Credit (DTC)
entries.description: A non-refundable tax credit that helps people with disabilities, or their supporting family member, reduce the amount of income tax they may have to pay. People with a severe and prolonged impairment apply to the Canada Revenue Agency with a 2-part application (Form T2201, Disability Tax Credit Certificate), sent through the digital application or by mail, and medical practitioners can complete their part digitally.
entries.cost_note: The page does not mention any fee to apply.
entries.evidence: If you have a severe and prolonged impairment, you may apply for the credit.
entries.notes: DTC approval is needed for the Canada Disability Benefit, the Child Disability Benefit and an RDSP (per those programs' pages). The page says DTC forms cannot be sent through the 'submit documents' section of a CRA account. Free application help: see the Inclusion Canada, Pathway to Benefits and Plan Institute entries. No phone number on the page. Page dated 2025-09-16.

entries.name: Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP)
entries.description: A long-term savings plan to help people with disabilities who are approved for the Disability Tax Credit save for the future; family income and contributions determine how much the plan could get in matching grants and bonds. A plan can be opened for an eligible beneficiary directly at a financial organization.
entries.cost_note: Savings plan opened at a financial organization; the page does not mention fees.
entries.evidence: A plan can be opened for an eligible beneficiary directly at a financial organization.
entries.notes: The page links to separate sections on grant and bond amounts. No phone number on the page (contact form only). For free help, see the Plan Institute helpline entry. Page dated 2026-07-10.

entries.name: Child Disability Benefit (CDB)
entries.description: A tax-free monthly payment for families who care for a child under 18 who is eligible for the Disability Tax Credit. Families must be eligible for the Canada child benefit, and those already getting it for a child approved for the DTC receive the payment automatically without applying.
entries.cost_note: Federal benefit paid to families; the page does not mention any fee.
entries.evidence: tax-free monthly payment made to families who care for a child under age 18
entries.notes: Phone is for general CDB questions; the page gives 1-800-959-8281 for Disability Tax Credit questions. This is separate from the adult Canada Disability Benefit. Page dated 2026-06-15.

entries.name: Jordan's Principle
entries.description: Jordan's Principle helps First Nations children get products, services and supports they need, such as speech therapy, educational supports, medical equipment and mental health services. Requests can be made through an online form or the call centre, and regional focal points and service coordinators help families submit a request for free.
entries.cost_note: The page says there is no fee for First Nations children to access Jordan's Principle.
entries.evidence: Regional focal points and service coordinators will help you submit a request for free.
entries.notes: Phone is 1-855-JP-CHILD; TTY 1-866-553-0554. The call centre is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week but is not a crisis line (call 911 in an emergency). Requests for Inuit children go through the Inuit Child First Initiative. Indigenous Services Canada page (canada.ca/en/indigenous-services-canada/services/jordans-principle.html redirects here), modified 2026-08-20. The page states no age range.

entries.name: Barrier-Free Benefits navigators (Inclusion Canada)
entries.description: Inclusion Canada's navigators give free, one-on-one help with disability benefits, including the Disability Tax Credit and its medical certificate, the Registered Disability Savings Plan and the Canada Disability Benefit, and can help gather documents and appeal decisions. People book an appointment online, and Ontario is served by the Central region (Manitoba and Ontario) navigator.
entries.cost_note: The page offers FREE one-on-one help and a free meeting.
entries.evidence: FREE, one-on-one help with disability benefits
entries.notes: Phone and email are for the Central region (Manitoba, Ontario), printed on inclusioncanada.ca/page/contact-navigators. The page does not say whether meetings are by phone, video or in person. Inclusion Canada is on the Government of Canada's list of funded disability benefits navigation organizations: https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/programs/social-development-partnerships/disabilities/organizations-benefits.html

entries.name: Pathway to Benefits (Mood Disorders Society of Canada)
entries.description: A free national initiative led by Mood Disorders Society of Canada to help Canadians with disabilities and their families apply for disability benefits, including the Canada Disability Benefit, the Disability Tax Credit and other provincial and territorial supports. It offers one-on-one support, online resources and peer guidance, including help with appeals and documentation.
entries.cost_note: The page says Pathway to Benefits is here to help at no cost.
entries.evidence: Pathway to Benefits is a free, national initiative led by Mood Disorders Society of Canada
entries.notes: Contact by phone, text or email. The site's call link dials 1-800-975-9990 while the printed number is 1-888-975-9990; the Government of Canada's disability benefits navigation page also lists 1-888-975-9990. Funded by the Government of Canada's Social Development Partnerships Program.

entries.name: Disability Planning Helpline (Plan Institute)
entries.description: Plan Institute's national helpline gives free one-on-one support on the Disability Tax Credit (including application support), the Registered Disability Savings Plan and the Canada Disability Benefit. People call toll-free from anywhere in Canada and leave a message; advisors usually reply within 4 to 8 business days, and interpreted support is available in ASL and other languages.
entries.cost_note: The page says using the helpline is completely free of charge.
entries.evidence: Using our Disability Planning Helpline is completely free of charge.
entries.notes: Help is by phone. The email address is hidden on the page, so it is left blank. Plan Institute also runs RDSP.com (step-by-step RDSP guide, tutorial, calculator and free webinars; the site says all of its services are free). Listed on the Government of Canada's disability benefits navigation page.

entries.name: Disability Benefits Compass (Prosper Canada)
entries.description: An online tool from Prosper Canada, a national charity, with information about the key disability benefits in each province and territory, including the Canada Disability Benefit, Disability Tax Credit, Registered Disability Savings Plan, Canada Pension Plan disability benefit and the Ontario Disability Support Program. It gives a step-by-step guide on how to apply, for people with disabilities, their caregivers and family members, and agency workers who help them.
entries.cost_note: The pages do not mention any fees.
entries.evidence: Providing information about the five key disability benefits for persons with disabilities in your province or territory.
entries.notes: Site name is Disability Benefits Compass, at disability.benefitswayfinder.org. Its About page describes a step-by-step guide on how to apply and says the project is funded in part by the Government of Canada's Social Development Partnerships Program. Prosper Canada's general Benefits Wayfinder (benefitswayfinder.org) also has Ontario pages, for example on ACSD.

entries.name: Benefits Finder (Government of Canada)
entries.description: A Government of Canada online tool that helps you find federal programs and benefits, with filters that include Disability as a support type and People with disabilities as an audience. It shows federal benefits only and links to provincial and territorial benefits websites.
entries.cost_note: The page does not mention any cost.
entries.evidence: The Benefits Finder helps you find federal programs and benefits.
entries.notes: Page dated 2026-04-16.

entries.name: Free tax clinics (Community Volunteer Income Tax Program)
entries.description: Free tax clinics where volunteers complete tax returns for people with a modest income and a simple tax situation, through the Community Volunteer Income Tax Program. The Find a free tax clinic tool lets you choose a clinic by location and the type of clinic you prefer.
entries.cost_note: The page describes them as free tax clinics.
entries.evidence: volunteers complete tax returns for people with a modest income and a simple tax situation
entries.notes: A filed tax return is needed for benefits such as the Canada Disability Benefit (per its eligibility page). The page gives no income limits and does not say whether clinics are in person or virtual. Page dated 2026-02-19.

entries.name: Community legal clinics (Legal Aid Ontario)
entries.description: Community-based legal clinics, funded by Legal Aid Ontario, give legal help to people with low incomes in Ontario, including on income support such as Ontario Works and the Ontario Disability Support Program (ODSP). Each clinic sets its own eligibility guidelines, and you can find your local clinic by address or postal code on Legal Aid Ontario's site.
entries.cost_note: The page says you may qualify for free legal services at a community legal clinic; eligibility is based on low income.
entries.evidence: Income support, such as Ontario Works, the Ontario Disability Support Program (ODSP), and Employment Insurance (EI).
entries.notes: Phone is Legal Aid Ontario's toll-free line (Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.); the legal clinics page also gives 416-979-1446 for Toronto and the GTA. Find a clinic: https://www.legalaid.on.ca/legal-clinics/ . Some specialty clinics serve specific groups, including people with disabilities.

entries.name: Awards and Funding (Autism Ontario)
entries.description: Autism Ontario's awards and funding page for adults lists its Building Brighter Futures Fund, which gives financial assistance directly to autistic adults in Ontario (successful lottery applicants can be reimbursed up to $500, once per person), along with scholarships. It also outlines government funding options for autistic and/or disabled adults, such as ODSP, Developmental Services Ontario Passport funding, the Disability Tax Credit and the RDSP.
entries.cost_note: The page does not mention application fees.
entries.evidence: provide financial assistance directly to autistic adults in Ontario
entries.notes: The BBFF page (autismontario.com/BBFF) says 2026 receipts are accepted from January 1 to September 30, 2026. The linked page on government funding for adults (…/awards-and-funding/government-funding-adults) also covers the Canada Disability Benefit and Henson trusts. Education scholarship applications were accepted online April 1 to 30, 2026. No phone or email on the page.

entries.name: Summer One to One Support Worker Reimbursement Fund (Autism Ontario)
entries.description: An Autism Ontario fund that helps parents pay for a support worker to go with their child (up to their 18th birthday) to a camp, program or community outings in July and August, reimbursing up to $600 per child. Applications with proof of an autism spectrum disorder diagnosis are taken online in May and entered into a random draw, and parents pay the worker first and then send paid-in-full receipts.
entries.cost_note: Reimbursement fund; the FAQ says Autism Ontario membership is not required and does not mention an application fee.
entries.evidence: The Fund is intended to help parents pay for a support worker to accompany the child to a camp/program
entries.notes: The fund page (autismontario.com/camp) says the 2026 fund is closed and to check back around May 1 to May 31, 2027. Only the support worker is reimbursed, not camp or program fees. The diagnosis must be on professional letterhead, signed by a qualified medical professional; families funded from 2007 to 2026 do not need to resubmit it.

entries.name: Equipment Funding Program (Easter Seals Ontario)
entries.description: Helps families with the cost of equipment needed by children and youth under 19 who are registered with Easter Seals Ontario and have a permanent physical disability that restricts their independent mobility, such as mobility devices, communication and writing aids, bathing and toileting aids, ramps and van lifts. Families send an Equipment Funding Application by email, mail or fax, and funding is up to $3,000 per child per calendar year while funds last.
entries.cost_note: Families are asked to contribute about $100 per request where possible; funding is limited and approved first come, first served.
entries.evidence: helps families with the cost of equipment that is required by children and youth with physical disability
entries.notes: Also 416-421-8146. Applicants must live in Ontario with a current health card, equipment must be on the Approved Equipment List, and applications must arrive 6 months before the child's 19th birthday. Decisions take about 6 to 8 weeks. Applications are accepted January 1 to December 31 or until funds run out.

entries.name: Home and Vehicle Modification Program (March of Dimes Canada)
entries.description: A means-tested March of Dimes Canada program for Ontario residents in financial need that funds basic, essential devices, adaptations, and home and vehicle modifications that remove a barrier related to the applicant's disability. Applicants must first try other public or private funding, then send the application with proof of income, an occupational therapist assessment or verification of disability form, and a price quote.
entries.cost_note: Means-tested; the application form says requests over $15,000 need a clear plan to pay that amount.
entries.evidence: this is a means tested Program intended to serve Ontario residents in the greatest financial need
entries.notes: The program's web pages (https://www.marchofdimes.ca/en-ca/programs/am/hvmp) block automated fetches, so this entry was checked against the program's own application form (dated 10/25) and devices list on marchofdimes.ca. Mailing address on the form: March of Dimes Canada, 595 Bradley Ave, Unit 202, London, ON N6E 3Z8; fax 519-432-4923. The devices list is about physical barriers at home related to mobility limitations (for example stairlifts, ramps and ceiling track lifts).

entries.name: Family Financial Support (Jennifer Ashleigh Children's Charity)
entries.description: Jennifer Ashleigh Children's Charity gives family financial support when an Ontario child (up to their 19th birthday) has had a major medical event needing a hospital stay of at least 2 weeks, for costs such as accommodation, transportation, medications and medical supplies, equipment, therapy fees, sibling childcare and 1:1 respite care. Household income must be $99,999 or less, and families or a healthcare worker apply online with a hospital letter of support and the latest Notice of Assessment.
entries.cost_note: Charity financial support; the page does not mention an application fee.
entries.evidence: Application may be completed by the family or a healthcare worker on their behalf.
entries.notes: Shorter hospital stays may be considered case by case if followed by intensive day or outpatient treatment. The child must be a permanent resident or Canadian citizen, with one application per child every 12 months; the 2025 Notice of Assessment is currently accepted. General email admin@jenash.org.

unverified.name: Respite Services (RespiteServices.com)
unverified.reason: Its own site (respiteservices.com) says it has not been operational since April 1, 2025, after the Geneva Centre ended its role as host; it no longer mentions SSAH, Passport or other funding help.

unverified.name: President's Choice Children's Charity
unverified.reason: Its own site (pcchildrenscharity.ca) now describes only its Power Full Kids food programs; no grant or application for children with disabilities was found there, so older reports of disability grants could not be confirmed.
